0.body: Welcome to the Relift documentation. Relift is a free, open-source, read-only deleted-file recovery tool for disk images and drives. Preview status. Validation is limited to deterministic synthetic fixtures. No physical drive or representative recovery corpus has been validated. Release binaries are unsigned. See Verification for the current evidence boundary.
0.title: Relift Documentation

1.body: Relift scans disk images and raw devices without writing to them, records what it finds in a session directory, and recovers validated byte ranges only to a separate destination. Unsupported filesystems and unvalidated carves are reported, never silently presented as recovered.
1.title: What Relift Does

10.body: Image a raw device (recommended over scanning a mounted volume): relift image \\.\PhysicalDrive1 --dest D:\images\evidence.dd Scan the image: relift scan D:\images\evidence.dd --session D:\session --live --carve Recover deleted files to a separate destination: relift recover D:\session --dest D:\recovered
10.breadcrumbs: Quick Start » Scan a Disk Image
10.title: Scan a Disk Image

101.body: ZIP64: shares the PK\x03\x04 local-header magic with ZIP and is validated by the existing ZIP validator rather than a separate carver. A dedicated ZIP64 end-of-central-directory validator is not yet implemented. The registry also contains marker-only entries that do not emit candidates. Available validators must accept the structure before any carve is emitted; validator coverage and maturity vary by format.
101.breadcrumbs: Limitations » Formats without a dedicated validator
101.title: Formats without a dedicated validator

102.body: Bifragment gap carving is not implemented for most formats. Fragmented MP4/MOV (moof/mdat) chains are not reassembled. JPEG recovery after a large non-JPEG gap is heuristic and may truncate or over-extend.
102.title: Fragmentation

103.body: Per-format size caps are enforced by each validator; files exceeding the cap are not carved. See the constants in crates/relift-core/src/carve.rs.
103.title: Limits

105.body: Raw physical disk access requires administrator elevation. Non-elevated runs list drive letters only and warn. GUI requires the WebView2 runtime (included in Windows 10 1809+).
105.title: Windows

106.body: Raw-device destination safety fails closed; imaging is recommended. Full Disk Access is required for raw devices. Raw-device paths have not been exercised in this repository. No signing/notarization: Gatekeeper warnings are expected.
106.title: macOS

107.body: Raw block devices normally require root. No io_uring or O_DIRECT path; reads use ordinary positioned file I/O. LVM/RAID reconstruction is not implemented.
107.title: Linux

109.body: A destination on the same physical device as the source is refused. Network and FUSE destinations are allowed but atomicity is not guaranteed.
109.title: Destination safety

11.body: If a scan was interrupted, resume it (the source must be unchanged): relift scan image.dd --session ./session --resume
11.breadcrumbs: Quick Start » Continue an Interrupted Scan
11.title: Continue an Interrupted Scan

110.body: SHA-256 is computed by default; --no-verify disables the re-read check. Failed-output handling differs by platform: Windows removes a failed output; Linux and macOS retain a collision-safe .partial file when possible. Sparse holes are written as zeroes and included in the hash.
110.title: Verification

111.body: Interrupted copies can resume from a durable prefix checkpoint with relift image --resume. Checkpoints are 256 MiB apart by default; uncommitted bytes are recopied. Resume hashes the saved prefix and re-reads the same source range to ensure the bytes still match. Imaging stops on unreadable source ranges. It does not record bad-sector ranges, retry sectors, or run multiple passes.
111.title: Imaging

112.body: Sessions are directories with session.json, candidates.jsonl, and recovered.jsonl; they do not use SQLite. Completed sessions can be listed, recovered, and reported later. A cancelled or crashed scan can be continued with relift scan --resume; the checkpoint is volume-level, so the interrupted volume is rescanned from its start. Recovery refuses a source whose size or fingerprint no longer matches the identity recorded in the session. Scan resume applies the same check.
112.title: Sessions

113.body: No published benchmark results exist yet. Run cargo bench -p relift-bench on your hardware and record the environment described in docs/benches/METHODOLOGY.md. Carving is single-pass and bounded-memory; very large images are processed incrementally rather than mapped whole.
113.title: Performance

124.body: All validation evidence above is against deterministic synthetic fixtures. No physical drive, deleted volume, or representative real-media recovery corpus has been validated. Claims about real-world recovery accuracy (precision, recall, F1) are not made and must not be made until a labelled ground-truth corpus is established (see docs/GAP_REPORT.md).
124.title: Validation boundary

125.body: Relift has not been evaluated in a reproducible, head-to-head recovery study. The repository contains deterministic synthetic fixtures, not a representative corpus of deleted files or measurements against other products. This page therefore does not rank recovery tools or claim that Relift is faster, more accurate, safer in practice, or more complete than another product.
125.title: Recovery Tool Comparison

126.body: FAT12/16/32, exFAT, NTFS, and ext2/3/4 have synthetic fixture tests. HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, and XFS are experimental and lack fixture validation. Carved candidates are emitted only after a format-specific validator accepts them; that does not establish recovery accuracy on real-world data. Recovery and imaging write to a validated destination path; raw-device behavior has not been tested against physical disks. The CLI can export JSON, HTML, and CSV reports. The GUI covers a subset of CLI capabilities. See support-matrix.md and VERIFICATION.md for the evidence and gaps.
126.breadcrumbs: Comparison » What has evidence in this repository
126.title: What has evidence in this repository

127.body: Compare the exact filesystem, deletion/format scenario, image format, and platform you need. Use a disposable test image with known file contents, record which files each tool restores byte-for-byte, and publish the test image, commands, tool versions, and system profile. Do not compare headline format counts or scan speed unless the inputs and validation rules are equivalent. For a failing or irreplaceable drive, stop using it and consider a professional recovery service. Relift is not certified for forensic evidence acquisition, partition repair, RAID reconstruction, or encrypted-volume recovery.
127.breadcrumbs: Comparison » How to compare tools for a recovery case
127.title: How to compare tools for a recovery case

130.body: Relift scans raw disk images and raw devices for recoverable filesystem metadata and structurally validated file signatures. It stores findings in a session directory, then can write selected files to a separate destination. The main workflows are documented in CLI.md .
130.title: What does Relift do?

131.body: FAT12/16/32, exFAT, NTFS, and ext2/3/4 have deterministic synthetic fixture coverage. HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, and XFS parsers are experimental and have not been validated against fixtures or real volumes. See the support matrix .
131.title: Which filesystems are supported?

132.body: Relift emits only formats with structural validators. The current list and known omissions are in support-matrix.md . A recognized signature alone is not enough to emit a candidate.
132.breadcrumbs: FAQ » What file types can it carve?
132.title: What file types can it carve?

133.body: Scanning uses a read-only source interface. Recovery and imaging write to separate destination paths. Always confirm that the destination is on a different physical volume, and run recovery with --dry-run first. Do not let an agent access a physical device without first confirming the source and destination with a human.
133.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Does Relift write to the source?
133.title: Does Relift write to the source?

134.body: Sometimes, if the content has not been erased or overwritten. TRIM and garbage collection often make deleted SSD content unrecoverable. Relift does not determine that data is recoverable just because metadata remains.
134.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Can I recover deleted data from an SSD?
134.title: Can I recover deleted data from an SSD?

135.body: If sectors were overwritten or discarded, their previous bytes cannot be recovered by software. A quick format may leave some metadata or content; a full overwrite generally does not.
135.breadcrumbs: FAQ » What happens after a format or overwrite?
135.title: What happens after a format or overwrite?

136.body: No. Relift does not crack or bypass encryption and does not reconstruct RAID, LVM, or other multi-device volumes. Decrypt or assemble the source with authorized tools first, then provide a supported raw image or device.
136.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Does Relift support encryption or RAID reconstruction?
136.title: Does Relift support encryption or RAID reconstruction?

137.body: No. Convert those containers to a raw image before scanning. Only raw images are supported directly.
137.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Can it read E01, VHD, VMDK, QCOW2, or DMG images?
137.title: Can it read E01, VHD, VMDK, QCOW2, or DMG images?

138.body: Stop using it. If it is clicking, beeping, disconnecting, or returning repeated read errors, consider professional recovery. Relift's image command can resume from durable checkpoints, but it does not provide unreadable-sector maps, retries, or multi-pass recovery. Image to a different physical volume before scanning when the device is stable enough to read.
138.breadcrumbs: FAQ » How do I handle a failing drive?
138.title: How do I handle a failing drive?

139.body: Relift cannot pause a running scan. If a scan is cancelled or the process crashes, relift scan <source> --session <dir> --resume continues it after revalidating the source. Completed volumes are skipped and the interrupted volume is rescanned from its start, so that volume's candidates are regenerated rather than duplicated. The GUI can stop a scan but does not expose resume.
139.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Can I pause or resume a scan?
139.title: Can I pause or resume a scan?

14.body: Code Meaning 0 OK 1 Runtime error 2 Usage error 3 Unsafe destination (same physical device) 4 Source mismatch (session vs actual source) 5 Partial recovery See docs/CLI.md for the full command reference.
14.title: Exit Codes

141.body:
relift scan image.dd --session ./session --mode quick
relift list ./session
relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery --dry-run Review the dry-run output, confirm the destination is on a separate physical volume, then run recovery without --dry-run.
141.breadcrumbs: FAQ » How do I start with an image?
141.title: How do I start with an image?

142.body: relift scan image.dd --session ./session --mode deep Deep mode includes metadata scanning and validated signature carving. Carved files may be partial, especially when the original file was fragmented or overwritten.
142.breadcrumbs: FAQ » How do I scan for carved files?
142.title: How do I scan for carved files?

143.body: Use candidate IDs, extensions, confidence labels, or path/name filters. For example: relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery \ --filter 'ext:jpg,png,pdf' --min-confidence likely --dry-run The complete filter grammar is in CLI.md . Confidence labels are evidence categories, not probabilities or guarantees that an application can open the file.
143.breadcrumbs: FAQ » How do I select files to recover?
143.title: How do I select files to recover?

144.body: Yes. Recovery re-reads and SHA-256 checks output files by default. The --no-verify option disables that check. Relift does not verify files by comparing them with an original copy unless you supply that comparison separately.
144.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Does Relift verify recovered files?
144.title: Does Relift verify recovered files?

145.body: A session is a directory containing session.json, candidates.jsonl, recovered.jsonl, and a short README. It is not a SQLite database. Session fields are versioned; see CLI.md and the implementation overview in architecture.md .
145.breadcrumbs: FAQ » What is a session directory?
145.title: What is a session directory?

146.body: It runs local storage, hashing, and carving self-tests, checks telemetry/network status, and attempts a read-only open and 512-byte read from a platform-specific raw-device path. It may therefore access a physical device; do not run it on behalf of someone else without confirming first.
146.breadcrumbs: FAQ » What does relift doctor check?
146.title: What does relift doctor check?

148.body: Yes. The desktop app uses Tauri 2 and Svelte 5. It covers source selection, scanning, result review, preview, and recovery. Imaging and report format selection are currently CLI-only. See GUI.md .
148.title: Is there a GUI?

149.body: No. The supported interfaces are the CLI and desktop GUI. relift self-update is not implemented.
149.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Is there a TUI or self-update command?
149.title: Is there a TUI or self-update command?

150.body: The core and CLI have no network client or telemetry. No account or cloud service is required.
150.breadcrumbs: FAQ » Does Relift send files or telemetry over the network?
150.title: Does Relift send files or telemetry over the network?

151.body: The v0.1.0 preview is published with unsigned assets and a SHA256SUMS file. No stable, signed, or notarized release is available. Homebrew, winget, Scoop, AUR, Flatpak, and Snap submissions have not been completed. See GAP_REPORT.md .

No real physical drive, real deleted volume, labeled accuracy corpus, 24-hour fuzz campaign, or hardware performance target has been validated. Relift is not certified for forensic evidence acquisition; see forensic-use.md and VERIFICATION.md .

160.body: Documented gaps in Relift's current implementation. Each gap is honest, deliberate, and tracked.
160.title: Gap report

162.body: $ATTRIBUTE_LIST: multi-attribute records are not followed; only unnamed $DATA and resident data are recovered. Named alternate data streams: not recovered. Compression (LZ77) and EFS: not decoded; reported as unsupported when encountered. $UsnJrnl: journal not replayed. $I30 directory-index slack and $Recycle.Bin metadata are not parsed as separate sources.
162.title: NTFS

163.body: Inline data larger than the inode body (>60 bytes): not implemented. Encryption: encrypted inodes reported as unverified, not decrypted. bigalloc: filesystem refused as unsupported. Journal replay: not performed; orphan and deleted-inode recovery only.
163.title: ext2/3/4

164.body: Parsers are implemented and wired into scan. Deterministic probe fixtures now exist and are covered by end-to-end detection tests (probe_identifies_hfsplus, probe_identifies_apfs, probe_identifies_btrfs, probe_identifies_xfs). Metadata-based deleted-file recovery is not implemented; output is experimental and identified-only. APFS/Btrfs snapshots are not enumerated as separate recovery sources. XFS inode-number reconstruction is approximate for B+tree leaf records.
164.breadcrumbs: Gap Report » HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, XFS
164.title: HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, XFS

165.body: ZIP64: shares the PK\x03\x04 local-header magic with ZIP and is handled by the existing ZIP validator rather than a separate carver. A dedicated ZIP64 end-of-central-directory validator is not yet implemented. Every emitted carve must pass a structural validator; unvalidated carves are never emitted.
165.title: Carving gaps

166.body: Only raw images are supported. E01/Ex01, AFF4, VHD/VHDX, VMDK, QCOW2 and DMG/UDIF must be converted to raw before scanning. Imaging can resume from a versioned JSONL checkpoint map at durable prefix boundaries. Checkpoints default to 256 MiB; uncheckpointed bytes are recopied after interruption. Bad-sector retries, unreadable-range maps, multi-pass recovery, and ddrescue mapfile import/export are not implemented.
166.title: Image format gaps

167.body: Windows: raw physical disk enumeration requires elevation. Non-elevated sessions list drive letters only with an honest warning. Windows ARM64: no build or runtime testing yet. macOS: raw-device destination safety fails closed with imaging advice; macOS raw paths are untested. Linux: raw device access may require root. Destination separation resolves partition, stacked-device, and NVMe namespace ancestry through sysfs; virtual destinations whose physical backing cannot be proven are refused. Btrfs destinations are refused because mount metadata does not establish every device in a multi-device filesystem. No io_uring or O_DIRECT path. GUI bundles are unsigned: no Authenticode certificate, Apple Developer ID or notarization credentials are configured.
167.title: Platform gaps

168.body: npm audit (2026-11-15) reports one low-severity prototype-poisoning advisory in the transitive, development-only deepmerge dependency of @sveltejs/vite-plugin-svelte. The upstream advisory lists no patched version; the affected package is not part of the built desktop runtime. Recovery and imaging now walk canonical destination paths from the volume root with no-follow directory opens, retain directory handles, and create output relative to those handles. This blocks traversal through symlinked or replaced destination ancestors after validation. Linux and macOS finalization use no-replace rename; Windows uses a no-overwrite move while destination directory handles remain open. A local process with write access can still modify output data or cause denial of service, and recovery files are visible under their final names while being written. Windows removes failed recovery outputs relative to the open parent handle instead of moving them to .partial; Linux and macOS retain failed outputs under collision-safe .partial names when possible. No real NTFS/ext4 volumes available locally. All validation so far is against deterministic synthetic fixtures (FAT32, exFAT, NTFS, ext4) with SHA-256 byte comparison. Cross-platform CI builds and runs the synthetic test suite on macOS. This Windows development host cannot exercise macOS raw-device behavior, and no raw physical media has been validated on any platform. Public test images or real-volume validation still needed before claiming real-media recovery. cargo-fuzz harnesses for the signature carver and filesystem probes are checked in under fuzz/, and CI runs bounded fuzz executions on Linux runners (nightly + clang). Local Windows execution is blocked because the clang/libFuzzer runtime DLL is not installed on this host; the harnesses compile cleanly. A sustained 24-hour fuzz campaign and crash-minimized corpus remain pending CI execution. Code coverage is not measured in CI.

19.body:
Probe filesystems and write deleted-file candidates to a session directory. relift scan <SOURCE> --session <DIR> [OPTIONS] Option Description <SOURCE> Disk image path or raw device (e.g., image.dd, \\.\PhysicalDrive1) --session <DIR> New or empty directory for session output; an existing interrupted session with --resume (required) --resume Continue an interrupted session. Uses the session's recorded options and requires an unchanged source --mode <MODE> Scan preset: quick (metadata only) or deep (metadata + validating carving). Default: config value or quick. --live Also list files that are still allocated --no-live Disable live entries, including a config default --carve Run signature carving in addition to metadata recovery (implied by --mode deep) --no-carve Disable carving, including config and deep-mode defaults --volume <INDEX> Scan only this volume index (repeatable) --offset <BYTES> Manual volume offset in bytes (requires --length) --length <BYTES> Manual volume length in bytes (requires --offset) --max-candidates <N> Stop after this many candidates (default: config value or 1,000,000) --json Machine-readable JSON output Examples: # Quick metadata scan (never reads the whole volume)
relift scan /dev/sdb --session ./session # Deep scan with validating signature carving
relift scan image.dd --session ./session --mode deep # Continue a cancelled or crashed scan (the source must be unchanged)
relift scan image.dd --session ./session --resume # Scan only a specific volume index
relift scan /dev/sdb --session ./session --volume 2 # Manual volume range
relift scan image.dd --session ./session --offset 1048576 --length 1000000000 Resume semantics. The checkpoint advances only after a whole volume has been scanned and its candidates have been flushed to disk. --resume skips volumes already recorded as complete and rescans the interrupted volume from its start; candidates written after the last completed volume are discarded. The session's recorded options (carving, live entries, volume selection, manual range, candidate limit) are reused. The source is re-opened read-only and its size and sampled fingerprint must match the session, otherwise resume is refused with exit code 4. Live pause/resume is not supported. Interrupted image copies can continue with relift image --resume; unreadable-sector retries and multi-pass recovery are not implemented.
19.title: relift scan

2.body: Read-only by construction – ReadOnlySource exposes no write method; the engine cannot modify the source device Byte-for-byte recovery verified against synthetic fixtures with SHA-256 Filesystem metadata recovery – FAT12/16/32, exFAT, NTFS, ext2/3/4 (fixture-validated); HFS+, APFS, Btrfs and XFS parsers are implemented but experimental Signature carving – 153 registered identifiers, including marker-only entries; only validator-backed formats emit candidates, and validation maturity varies (full registry in Supported Formats ) Session-based workflow – scan → session → recover → report, with checkpoint resume Cross-platform – Windows, macOS, and Linux No telemetry – fully offline by default

20.body:
List candidates saved in a session without writing anything. relift list <SESSION> [OPTIONS] Option Description <SESSION> Session directory produced by relift scan --filter <EXPR> Filter candidates (repeatable): ext:jpg,png, format:pdf, name:IMG_, path:DCIM --min-confidence <LABEL> Hide candidates below this confidence (verified, likely, partial, unverified) --limit <N> Maximum rows to print (0 means all) (default: 100) --json Machine-readable JSON output Filter expressions: ext:jpg,png,mp4 # by file extension or filename extension
format:pdf # by recorded candidate format
name:IMG_ # case-insensitive filename substring
path:DCIM # case-insensitive path substring Multiple --filter expressions are ANDed; comma-separated values within one expression are ORed. Examples: # List all candidates (first 100)
relift list ./session # Only verified JPEGs and PNGs
relift list ./session --filter 'ext:jpg,png' --min-confidence verified # JSON output
relift list ./session --json
20.title: relift list

21.body:
Recover candidates from a session into a destination directory. The source's identity must still match the session record; a changed image is refused. relift recover <SESSION> --dest <DIR> [OPTIONS] Option Description <SESSION> Session directory produced by relift scan --dest <DIR> Destination directory (must be on a different physical device); can come from [output].dest --source <PATH> Re-open this source instead of the path recorded in the session --filter <EXPR> Filter candidates (repeatable): same expressions as relift list --dry-run Plan only: validate source and destination, list what would be written. No files are written and the session is not modified. --no-verify Do not re-read each output file after writing it (verification is on by default) --verify Re-read each output file, overriding a config setting that disables verification --min-confidence <LABEL> Skip candidates below this confidence (verified, likely, partial, unverified) --id <N> Recover only these candidate IDs (repeatable) --json Machine-readable JSON output Examples: # Recover all candidates
relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery # Only verified JPEGs, dry run first
relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery --filter 'ext:jpg' --min-confidence verified --dry-run # Recover specific IDs only
relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery --id 123 --id 456 # Without post-write hash verification
relift recover ./session --dest /mnt/recovery --no-verify
21.title: relift recover

22.body: Copy a source to a new image file and write a SHA-256 manifest. Existing files are never overwritten. relift image <SOURCE> --dest <FILE> [OPTIONS] Option Description <SOURCE> Disk image or raw device path --dest <FILE> New image file to create (never overwrites existing) --resume Resume from the last durable checkpoint in the existing .partial image and .relift-map.jsonl file --no-verify Do not re-read the finished image to verify its hash --json Machine-readable JSON output Example: relift image /dev/sdb --dest /mnt/backup/drive.img If imaging is interrupted, rerun the same command with --resume. Relift revalidates the source identity and checks the saved image prefix against the current source bytes before continuing. This re-reads the checkpointed prefix. Checkpoints are synced every 256 MiB by default; an interruption may require recopying bytes since the last checkpoint. --resume only applies to a Relift partial image and its matching map file. It does not retry unreadable sectors or provide ddrescue-style multi-pass recovery.

33.body: Relift's desktop interface uses Tauri 2 and Svelte 5. It calls the shared relift-core library through Tauri commands. The GUI is a subset of the CLI; see CLI.md for imaging, report export, shell completions, and other commands.
33.title: Desktop GUI

34.body: The first screen lists devices visible to the operating system and lets the user select a raw image file. It shows the device path, type, size, filesystem label when available, accessibility status, and any OS-provided note. It does not inspect SMART health or reliably determine SSD TRIM status. Only raw image files are supported directly. The safety notice recommends stopping use of the source and recovering to a different physical drive. If the source is failing, consider professional recovery or image it before scanning. Advanced options currently include: Quick scan: filesystem metadata. Deep scan: metadata plus validated signature carving. Include files that are still allocated. Formatted-partition recovery, lost-partition recovery, and worker-thread controls are not implemented.
34.title: Choose a source

35.body: The scan screen receives progress events from the running scan and displays phase, bytes processed, elapsed time, estimated throughput, ETA, and the number of candidates saved in the session. ETA and throughput are estimates, not promises. The user can stop the scan and keep results already written to the session. Live pause is not implemented, and the GUI does not expose the CLI's checkpoint-resume workflow. Candidates are reviewed after the scan finishes or is stopped. The GUI does not preview or recover candidates while scanning.
35.title: Scan

36.body: The results screen supports text search, type and confidence filters, sorting, selecting visible rows, and selecting Verified/Likely candidates. Its preview shows candidate metadata and validator notes; it does not render the recovered file contents. The user selects a destination folder and starts recovery. The shared recovery engine validates the destination and verifies output hashes by default. The GUI shows recovered, partial, failed, and byte counts when the operation finishes. Recovery destination safety is still subject to the platform limits in support-matrix.md .
36.title: Review and recover

37.body: No imaging workflow in the GUI; use relift image from the CLI. No report format picker in the GUI; use relift report from the CLI. No content viewer, folder-tree view, or 500,000-row performance claim. No pause/resume for a running scan, and no resume control in the GUI; the backend supports relift scan --resume from the CLI. No device-health, SMART, or TRIM diagnosis. The older screenshots in docs/assets/screenshots/ remain unverified and are not product evidence. A separate real-app capture set is recorded in GUI_CAPTURE.md and its provenance . Those captures use generated synthetic data; they do not establish recovery accuracy on real media. The GUI is built in the release workflow, but platform runtime behavior, accessibility, cold-start time, and large-result performance have not been measured as release gates. See VERIFICATION.md .
37.title: Current exclusions

38.body: This document summarizes what the current parsers implement. The status and test evidence are in the support matrix . A parser being present does not establish recovery accuracy on a real volume.
38.title: Filesystem support reference

40.body: The parser reads directory entries, long file names, and cluster chains. Deleted data may be incomplete when allocation metadata has been cleared or clusters have been reused. The short-name deletion marker loses its first byte.
40.title: FAT12, FAT16, FAT32

41.body: The parser reads directory entry sets and uses allocation metadata and the NoFatChain flag. Recovery can be incomplete when the expected FAT chain is unavailable or the file data has been overwritten.
41.title: exFAT

42.body: The parser reads MFT records, resident and non-resident unnamed data, runlists, and sparse runs. It does not follow ATTRIBUTE_LIST continuation records, recover named alternate data streams, decompress LZNT1, decrypt EFS, replay the USN journal or LogFile, or parse Recycle Bin metadata as a separate source.
42.title: NTFS

43.body: The parser reads inode metadata, supported block/extent mappings, directory entries, sparse extents, and unwritten extents. It does not replay the journal, recover inline data larger than 60 bytes, decrypt fscrypt data, or support bigalloc. Deletion and reuse can remove the metadata needed to locate content.
43.title: ext2, ext3, ext4

44.body: HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, and XFS parsers are wired into scanning. Deterministic probe fixtures and end-to-end detection tests exist (probe_identifies_hfsplus, probe_identifies_apfs, probe_identifies_btrfs, probe_identifies_xfs), but metadata-based deleted-file recovery has not been validated against a fixture or real volume. Treat recovery results as experimental. Snapshot enumeration, encryption, compression, hardlink resolution, and other filesystem-specific cases are incomplete; see limitations .
44.title: Experimental parsers

45.body: ReFS, F2FS, ZFS, ReiserFS, ISO 9660, and UDF may be identified by probing, but metadata recovery is not implemented.

48.body: Relift searches for registered signatures and emits a candidate only when the corresponding validator accepts the structure. 51.body: Validators enforce format-specific length, structure, checksum, and/or end marker rules where implemented. Validation depth differs by format and is not a substitute for a format library or application-level verification. Embedded compressed or encrypted content is recovered as bytes; Relift does not decrypt or extract it. The confidence labels are evidence categories, not probabilities. A validated fragment may still be incomplete because the source file was fragmented, overwritten, or truncated. Recovery SHA-256 verification checks that the bytes written to the destination match the bytes read back; it does not prove they match an original copy.
51.title: Validation limits

52.body: Follow the contribution guide and add valid, truncated, and malformed test fixtures before registering a new marker. Do not emit a format based only on a magic-byte match. The registered_format_count_is_stable unit test fails when the marker set changes, which is the prompt to update this page and the support matrix.
52.title: Adding a format

53.body: Relift is a data-recovery utility, not a certified forensic acquisition tool. It has no case-management mode, DFXML export, source-range hashing, investigator fields, hardware write-blocker control, or forensic-grade checkpointing. Scan resume is a crash-recovery convenience, not a chain-of-custody control. Do not describe its output as a validated forensic image or a complete chain-of- custody record. For legally or professionally consequential evidence, follow your organization's procedures and applicable standards. Use a hardware write blocker and a validated forensic acquisition tool when required. Have a qualified examiner review the acquisition and analysis plan.
53.breadcrumbs: Forensic Use » Forensic Use and Evidence Handling
53.title: Forensic Use and Evidence Handling

54.body:
Stop using the source device. Do not write recovered output back to it. Confirm the source and destination with the operator. The destination must be a different physical volume. If appropriate, create a raw image on the separate destination. Relift's image command writes a SHA-256 manifest and can resume from durable prefix checkpoints; it does not provide bad-sector maps, read retries, or multi-pass recovery, and is not a forensic acquisition substitute. Scan the image, review candidates, and run a dry-run recovery. Recover only after confirming the dry-run and destination. Keep the image, session directory, report, and recovered output under controlled storage. Example for an already-created raw image: relift scan /evidence/source.img --session /evidence/session --mode quick
relift list /evidence/session --json
relift recover /evidence/session --dest /recovery --dry-run
# After reviewing the plan and confirming /recovery is a separate physical volume:
relift recover /evidence/session --dest /recovery
relift report /evidence/session --format json --out /evidence/report.json For metadata plus carving, use --mode deep. Raw device paths, permissions, and destination checks vary by operating system; see support-matrix.md .
54.title: Safer recovery workflow

55.body: The session directory stores a versioned JSON header, candidate JSONL records, recovery-result JSONL records, and a README. The source identity uses a fingerprint derived from source size and sampled bytes; it is not a cryptographic hash of every source byte. Recovered output files are SHA-256 verified by default after writing. The image manifest contains the image copy's hash. These records are useful for repeatable recovery work, but are not a tamper-proof audit log and do not replace independent evidence acquisition, full-source hashing, timestamps from a trusted clock, or examiner notes. Preserve copies and compute any hashes required by your procedure independently.
55.breadcrumbs: Forensic Use » What the session records
55.title: What the session records

56.body: The source abstraction is read-only, but this alone does not certify forensic soundness or prevent the operating system from changing a mounted source. Destination separation is checked by Relift where the platform can establish physical backing. Review warnings and do not use an ambiguous destination. Only raw disk images are supported directly; other containers must be converted with an appropriate tool. Filesystem recovery has deterministic synthetic-fixture evidence only. Real-media accuracy and forensic validation have not been established. Relift does not decrypt BitLocker, LUKS, or FileVault, reconstruct RAID, or repair partition tables. No --forensic, --case-id, --investigator, --verify, or DFXML export option exists. SHA-256 recovery verification is on by default and can be disabled with --no-verify. See limitations.md , GAP_REPORT.md , and VERIFICATION.md for current support and evidence status.
56.title: Important limits

57.body: Use the command reference in CLI.md for available flags. Relift does not implement --max-mem, --threads, --rate-limit, bad-sector map files, or a forensic mode. Scan and image resume are available through scan --resume and image --resume; neither is a live pause control.
57.title: Troubleshooting

58.body: Raw-device access may require Administrator on Windows or elevated permissions on Linux and macOS. Prefer a raw image when possible. Only raw image files are supported; convert E01/AFF4/VHD/VMDK/QCOW2/DMG containers before scanning. relift devices lists devices visible to the operating system. relift doctor runs local self-tests and also attempts a read-only open and a 512-byte read from a platform-specific raw-device path. Confirm with the device owner before running it on a system with physical media attached.

60.body:
Run a quick metadata scan first. If it finds nothing and the filesystem or source is suitable, a deep scan also runs the supported signature validators: relift scan image.dd --session ./session --mode quick
relift scan image.dd --session ./deep-session --mode deep Deleted content may already have been overwritten or erased by SSD TRIM. A full overwrite cannot be reversed. Encrypted volumes are not decrypted by Relift.

60.title: The scan finds no candidates

61.body: Use a new or empty directory for --session. A scan does not overwrite an existing session's files.
61.breadcrumbs: Troubleshooting » The session directory is not empty
61.title: The session directory is not empty

62.body: Candidates already written to the session are retained. Continue the same session with relift scan <source> --session <dir> --resume; the source must be unchanged. Resume skips volumes already completed and rescans the interrupted volume from its start, discarding candidates written after the last completed volume. The GUI's stop action cancels scanning and keeps the results already recorded; it has no resume control.
62.title: The scan is interrupted

63.body: Relift compares source size and fingerprint with the session. If they differ, re-scan the current image into a new session. The --source option can select the intended source path, but does not bypass the identity check.
63.breadcrumbs: Troubleshooting » The source changes before recovery
63.title: The source changes before recovery

65.body: Choose a directory on a different physical volume. Some virtual, stacked, or multi-device destinations are refused when Relift cannot prove their physical backing. Use an ordinary local volume or a raw image as the source. Run recovery with --dry-run first. Confirm the destination is a separate physical volume before writing.
65.title: The destination is rejected

66.body: Content can be incomplete if the original file was fragmented, overwritten, truncated, or only partially validated. Confidence labels describe the available recovery evidence; they are not probabilities or guarantees that an application can open the file. SHA-256 verification checks that output bytes were written consistently, not that they match an unavailable original.
66.breadcrumbs: Troubleshooting » A recovered file is partial or will not open
66.title: A recovered file is partial or will not open

67.body: Inspect the JSON or human-readable recovery summary and run relift report <SESSION> --format json. Linux and macOS may retain a failed output under a collision-safe .partial name; Windows removes failed output.
67.breadcrumbs: Troubleshooting » Recovery stops with an error
67.title: Recovery stops with an error

68.body: relift image creates a new raw image and refuses to overwrite an existing destination. If a run was interrupted, use the same source and destination with --resume; Relift checks the source identity and verifies the saved checkpoint prefix against both the partial image and current source bytes before continuing. This re-reads the checkpointed source range. It does not retry bad sectors or perform multiple recovery passes. For a failing or physically damaged drive, stop using it and consider professional recovery or a dedicated imaging tool designed for read errors.

71.body: Relift is a Rust workspace with one shared recovery library, a native CLI, a Tauri desktop application, deterministic test fixtures, and a Criterion benchmark crate. The CLI and GUI call the same relift-core APIs.
71.title: Architecture

72.body: flowchart LR A[Image or raw device] --> B[Read-only source] B --> C[Partition and filesystem probes] C --> D[Metadata scan] C --> E[Validated carving when requested] D --> F[Candidate session] E --> F F --> G[CLI or GUI review] G --> H[Destination validation] H --> I[Recovery writer] I --> J[Output hash verification] B --> K[Imaging command] K --> L[New raw image and manifest]
72.title: Data flow

73.body: Crate Responsibility relift-core Read-only sources, device enumeration, partition and filesystem parsing, carving validation, sessions, safe recovery and imaging writers, reports relift-cli devices, scan, list, recover, image, doctor, report, version, and shell completion commands relift-gui Tauri 2 commands and Svelte 5 interface backed by relift-core relift-testkit Deterministic synthetic disk and filesystem fixtures used by tests relift-bench Criterion microbenchmarks; results are not a substitute for real-media performance measurements
73.title: Crate responsibilities

74.body: ReadOnlySource provides positional reads and identity information but has no write operation. The CLI and GUI open regular image files or platform raw devices through this abstraction. Raw-device access and physical-disk identification have platform-specific limits described in support-matrix.md . The scanner probes partitions and supported filesystems. Quick mode scans metadata; deep mode also runs the signature validators. Metadata and carve results become Candidate records with source locations, extents, recovery method, and confidence. Experimental parsers are listed separately from fixture-validated filesystems.
74.title: Source and scan path

75.body: A session is a directory, not a database: session.json stores schema version, source identity, scan options, summary, filesystem reports, warnings, and recovery totals. candidates.jsonl stores one candidate per line and is appended as results are produced. recovered.jsonl records recovery results. README.txt describes the session. Candidate records stream to disk rather than being accumulated into one in-memory result list. A completed session can be listed, recovered, or reported again. session.json also stores a volume-level checkpoint: after a volume's metadata and carving work is flushed and synced, the checkpoint records the volume index and the durable length of candidates.jsonl. relift scan --resume truncates back to that boundary, rebuilds the summary from the surviving records, and continues. The interrupted volume is rescanned from its start; there is no chunk-level checkpoint.
75.title: Session format

76.body: The recovery path opens and validates the source, compares its identity with the session, validates the destination, then writes only under the selected destination directory. Destination handling uses anchored directory handles, no-follow path traversal, and collision-safe file creation/finalization. On supported platforms, same-device destinations are rejected; cases whose physical backing cannot be proven fail closed. Platform details and remaining limits are in GAP_REPORT.md . Recovered files are re-read and SHA-256 checked by default. --no-verify disables this post-write check. The image command copies from a read-only source to a new raw image destination and writes a SHA-256 manifest; it does not overwrite an existing destination.
76.title: Recovery and imaging writes

77.body: The CLI exposes the complete current command set and machine-readable JSON. The GUI covers source selection, scanning, result review, preview, and recovery. Imaging, report-format selection, and checkpoint resume remain CLI-only. The GUI can stop a scan and keep partial results; it does not pause a running scan. See CLI.md and GUI.md for user-facing behavior.
77.title: Interfaces

78.body: Tests prove behavior on deterministic synthetic fixtures, including byte-level recovery comparisons and destination safety cases. CI builds and tests the workspace on Windows, macOS, and Linux. No real physical disk or real deleted volume has been validated yet; no accuracy percentage or hardware performance target is claimed. See VERIFICATION.md .
78.title: Verification boundaries

81.body: When publishing numbers, include: Commit SHA and release version. CPU, RAM, storage model and interface (for example NVMe 4.0). Operating system and kernel version. Rust version and build profile (release, LTO settings). Image size, filesystem and candidate count. Command line used. Wall time, throughput, peak RSS, candidate count, verified count. Use the methodology in docs/benches/METHODOLOGY.md so results are comparable.
81.title: Recording a result

82.body: relift-bench includes Criterion groups for: Signature sweep throughput on a synthetic buffer with many false positives. Validator throughput for representative carved formats. Metadata scan throughput on generated FAT32, exFAT, NTFS and ext4 fixtures. Filesystem probe throughput. These are smoke/regression benchmarks, not a published performance claim. The CI workflow runs a benchmark smoke test on a schedule; it does not publish or compare results against a hosted baseline.
82.title: Current benchmark groups

84.body: Relift reads disk images and raw devices that may contain corrupt or hostile metadata. It writes recovered files or images only under a user-selected destination. The source, session, command-line paths, and file contents are untrusted inputs. Relift is not a certified forensic tool and does not defend against a compromised operating system or a local process that controls the destination volume.
84.title: Scope and assumptions

85.body: Source integrity: scanning and imaging must not write to the source. Destination confinement: recovered paths must remain inside the chosen destination and must not overwrite an existing file unexpectedly. Recovered-data integrity: report successful output verification and distinguish partial or failed recovery. User privacy: do not send device data, file contents, or telemetry over the network. Process stability: reject malformed offsets and structures safely and avoid unbounded result accumulation where the session writer can stream data.
85.title: Assets

87.body: The core scanner accepts a ReadOnlySource with no write operation. Imaging and recovery use explicit destination writers. Destination paths are opened component-by-component, without following links, and retained as handles while output is created. Output files use collision-safe creation. Source identity is recorded in the session; recovery refuses a source whose size or fingerprint differs from the recorded source. Platform-specific physical-device checks reject known same-device recovery destinations. When backing cannot be proven, supported paths fail closed. Recovered output is SHA-256 checked by default. The user can disable the post-write read-back check with --no-verify.
87.title: Source and destination

88.body: Parsers use bounded reads and checked range validation at input boundaries. Signature carving emits a candidate only when its format validator accepts the structure. Filesystem and carve limitations are recorded in the support matrix and gap report; a signature match alone is not represented as validated recovery. Candidate records stream to JSONL session files rather than being retained as one in-memory result set. --max-candidates limits the number of candidates. Recovered names are sanitized and destination traversal is rejected. See GAP_REPORT.md for platform-specific output behavior.
88.breadcrumbs: Threat Model » Parser and output handling
88.title: Parser and output handling

89.body: The core and CLI contain no network client or telemetry. The doctor command reports network/telemetry status but also attempts a read-only open and 512-byte read from a platform-specific raw-device path. cargo deny check runs in CI for dependency advisories, licenses, bans, and source configuration.
89.title: Privacy and dependencies

90.body: Synthetic tests do not prove safety against every malformed image or real device behavior. No comprehensive fuzz harness or 24-hour fuzz campaign is checked in. The Linux device-ancestry tests are synthetic; there has been no same-device refusal test against mounted physical disks. Raw-device behavior and physical destination checks are not validated on actual media. macOS raw-device access is untested and destination checks fail closed. Resource behavior on multi-terabyte images and very large candidate sets has not been profiled. There is no --max-mem or --timeout option. Scan resume is volume-level: an interrupted volume is rescanned from its start, and candidates written after the last completed volume are discarded. The source fingerprint samples head/tail bytes rather than hashing the whole source, so a change outside the sampled ranges is not detected. A process crash may leave partial destination output; failed-output cleanup differs by platform. A local process with write access to the destination can alter output or cause denial of service. No signed release artifacts or notarized GUI bundles exist. The published v0.1.0 preview has unsigned assets; its SHA256SUMS file does not authenticate the publisher.
90.breadcrumbs: Threat Model » Remaining threats and evidence gaps
90.title: Remaining threats and evidence gaps

91.body: Relift is a recovery utility, not an evidence-acquisition or chain-of-custody system. Session fingerprints sample the source rather than hashing every byte; session files are not tamper-evident. No case-management mode, DFXML export, or source-range hashing is implemented. For forensic use, follow organizational procedures, use an appropriate write blocker, and independently acquire and hash evidence with validated tools. See VERIFICATION.md for test results and release gates.
91.title: Forensic limits

92.body: This document lists current, verified limitations. It intentionally avoids claiming features that are not implemented. See docs/GAP_REPORT.md for the tracked work list.
92.title: Known Limitations

94.body: $ATTRIBUTE_LIST is not followed; only the base record's unnamed $DATA (resident or non-resident) is recovered. Named alternate data streams are not recovered. LZNT1 compression and EFS encryption are reported, not decoded. $LogFile and $UsnJrnl are not replayed. Hardlinks/reparse points are not resolved; only the first known name is used. $I30 index slack and $Recycle.Bin are not parsed as separate sources.
94.title: NTFS

95.body: A quick format zeroes the FAT; cluster chains are lost. Deleted files are assumed contiguous, which can truncate or over-extend output. The 0xE5 delete marker destroys the first short-name byte. LFN is used when available; otherwise the missing byte becomes _. Corrupt LFN checksums do not invalidate the decoded name; the checksum is treated as informational.
95.title: FAT12/16/32

96.body: NoFatChain is handled; when a FAT chain is expected but zeroed, recovery falls back to contiguous allocation and may be incomplete. The allocation bitmap is used for probing, not as a complete free-space map.
96.title: exFAT

97.body: Deletion commonly zeroes extent/block pointers. Recovery uses surviving inode fields, directory entries and contiguous-run heuristics. Inline data larger than the inode body (>60 bytes) is not recovered. fscrypt-encrypted inodes are reported as unverified, not decrypted. bigalloc is refused as unsupported. Journal replay is not performed.
97.title: ext2/3/4

98.body: Parsers are implemented and probe fixtures exist, but metadata-based deleted-file recovery has no deterministic end-to-end test yet. APFS/Btrfs snapshot trees are not enumerated as separate recovery sources. APFS clone extents and FileVault-encrypted volumes are not decoded. HFS+ journal replay and hardlink/alias resolution are not implemented. Btrfs compressed extents (zstd/lzo) are not decompressed. XFS inode numbers from B+tree leaves are approximate.
98.title: HFS+, APFS, Btrfs, XFS

99.body: Detection only. Metadata recovery is not implemented; raw carving may still find content on the underlying bytes.
